overview.body: This is a MASTER unit! You'll copy your Lab 1.2 code and add a second beach. Make it to Houston, and your program asks whether you want to keep going to Galveston. That's a decision inside a decision, plus two new Chapter 3 tools: the or operator and Boolean variables.

mentorQuote.quote: This is where it gets interesting. Your program now asks a question only some players ever see: you have to reach Houston first. Then the answer leads to one more decision inside that one. Read the indentation like an outline, and the whole decision tree is right there on the screen.

objectives: Start from your finished Lab 1.2 and add a closing line with the player's name
Check two cities at once with the or operator
Use a Boolean variable, reached_beach, to decide the status
Ask a question only in Houston with a nested if, and accept y or Y
Work out the last 50 miles to Galveston, three decisions deep
Test every outcome, including the ones you only reach by breaking the rules
overview.textbookReference: Starting Out with Python, 6th Edition by Tony Gaddis, Chapter 3: Decision Structures and Boolean Logic

content.body: Lab 1.3 adds a second beach, Galveston. Before anyone can get there, your ending has to know that Galveston counts as a beach. You'll rewrite the ending with or and a Boolean variable called reached_beach. Nothing the player sees changes in this checkpoint: every run prints exactly what it printed in CP1.

or lets one if check two things: the condition is true when either side is true. A Boolean variable holds True or False, a yes-or-no answer your program can check later. Changing how code works without changing what it prints is called refactoring, and running the same tests before and after is how you know nothing broke.

content.quote: When I first learned the or operator, I kept writing if current_city == 'Corpus Christi' or 'Galveston': and wondering why every single trip got the beach banner. You need the full comparison on both sides of the or. Trust me, this trips everyone up at first!

content.body: When the player makes it to Houston, the beach is only 50 more miles away. Your program asks whether they want to keep going. A y or Y sends them toward Galveston; any other answer, and they stay in Houston.

This question only makes sense once you're in Houston, so it's an if inside another if: the outer one checks where you are, and the inner one checks what the player typed. Python compares text exactly, so 'y' and 'Y' are different strings. or lets one check accept both.
